propositions.text: Heard claimant's evidence and reviewed personal information form and notes
propositions.quote: I have heard your evidence this morning concerning why you cannot return to Sri Lanka and I have reviewed your personal information form and my notes concerning your evidence.

propositions.text: Considered counsel's submissions and decided to reject the claim
propositions.quote: I have considered your counsel's submissions and these are the reasons why I reject your claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court heard the claimant's evidence, reviewed documents, considered counsel's submissions, and decided to reject the claim.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges targeting by LTTE and Sri Lankan security forces, leading to fleeing Sri Lanka
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that when she lived in XXXXX she was targeted by both the LTTE and the security forces of Sri Lanka and she was suspected by the security forces of supporting the LTTE and as a result of that ongoing suspicion and the problems that that caused her she decided that she must flee Sri Lanka

propositions.text: Claimant moved briefly to XXXXX and left Sri Lanka with agent's help using genuine passport and ID card
propositions.quote: she then moved for a short period of time to XXXXX and she alleges that with the help of an agent she left Sri Lanka using her genuine Sri Lankan passport and national identity card and went to Singapore.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges being targeted by LTTE and security forces, fled Sri Lanka, moved briefly to XXXXX, and left with agent's help using genuine documents.

propositions.text: In Singapore, claimant was given a new passport and gave genuine documents to agent
propositions.quote: While in Singapore she was provided with a new passport and handed her genuine passport and national identity card to her agent.

propositions.text: Claimant used new passport to travel to Japan and then Canada, making refugee claim two days after arrival
propositions.quote: She used the new passport to travel to Japan and from Japan to Canada, entering Canada by way of Pearson International Airport and two days later made a refugee claim inland in Etobicoke.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant got a new passport in Singapore, gave genuine documents to agent, traveled to Japan and Canada, and claimed refugee status two days after arrival.

propositions.text: Claimant entered Canada on October 5, 2009 and made refugee claim two days later
propositions.quote: She entered Canada on October 5, 2009; two days later made a refugee claim at the Etobicoke office asking for Canada's protection.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant entered Canada on October 5, 2009 and made a refugee claim two days later.

propositions.text: Credibility is the core issue, focusing on travel explanation and missing genuine documents
propositions.quote: The core of this claim is credibility and credibility comes from two basic concerns. The explanation as to how she travelled to Canada, the explanation for the missing genuine Sri Lankan passport and national identity card

propositions.text: Credibility concerns due to lack of supporting documents except proof claimant was in Sri Lanka at claimed times
propositions.quote: there are credibility concerns concerning her total lack of documents to support with one exception, that she was in Sri Lanka at the times she claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies credibility as the core issue, focusing on travel explanation and missing documents except proof of presence in Sri Lanka.

propositions.text: Claimant could not remember airlines or issuing country of fraudulent passport used in travel
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she left Sri Lanka with her genuine passport but was unable to remember the airline that she used for the trip to Singapore...unable to remember the country that had issued that fraudulent passport...unable to remember the airline that she used to travel from Singapore to Japan; she was unable to remember the airline she used to travel from Japan to Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant said agent used forged passport on her behalf for boarding and border controls
propositions.quote: She testified that she was never given that passport, that fraudulent passport but the agent used it on her behalf to get boarding passes at Singapore and Japan, to clear exit controls from Singapore, entry controls into Japan, exit controls from Japan and entry controls into Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant could not recall airlines or issuing country of forged passport, and said agent used it on her behalf for travel and border controls.

propositions.text: Counsel argues claimant's lack of memory is plausible due to agent control, urgency, and claimant's gender
propositions.quote: Counsel has submitted that because she was under the control of the agent she would perhaps not remember details. Counsel also submitted that she was fleeing for her life and her primary concern would be to escape Sri Lanka and she is a woman and it is plausible that she would not remember the airline or some other details about her trip.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel argues claimant's memory lapses are plausible due to agent control, urgency, and claimant being a woman.

propositions.text: Implausible claimant would not remember any travel details or forged document issuer
propositions.quote: I find it implausible that the claimant would not remember anything of her trip, any of the documents used or how they were used or at what times they were used on her trip to Canada. It is simply implausible that she would travel to Canada on a forged document and not know the country that issued the forged document.

propositions.text: Implausible claimant was not told forged document holder's name or that agent held documents at all times
propositions.quote: It is further implausible that she would not have been told the name of the holder of the forged document...The lack of knowledge of the forged document on its face does not appear to be consistent with the information she gave the immigration officer at question 19 of the schedule 1 on the claim for refugee protection found as part of Exhibit R-2.

propositions.text: Implausible agent held documents at all times without claimant possessing them during travel
propositions.quote: It is further implausible that the agent would be able to hold these documents at all times and not have her in possession of the document when boarding the plane or when going through the various controls at various airports.

propositions.text: Plausible claimant might forget some details but not all details of travel
propositions.quote: while I agree with counsel that it is plausible that a claimant of this age might not remember some of the details, I do not accept it as plausible that they would not remember any of the details.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it implausible claimant forgot all travel details or forged document info, rejecting counsel's partial memory argument.

propositions.text: Corrected counsel's estimate of claimant's time in Canada to 10 months
propositions.quote: Counsel submitted that the claimant came to Canada approximately a year ago. It was actually ... it is a much shorter period than that, after being corrected by counsel, I agree it was 10 months.

paragraphs.summary: The court corrected counsel's estimate, finding claimant has been in Canada about 10 months.

propositions.text: Claimant lacks documents to place herself in Sri Lanka except one document
propositions.quote: I asked the claimant a number of questions about documents that she might possibly have that would help her place herself in Sri Lanka when she claims...I have only one document that places her in Sri Lanka at the time she claims.

propositions.text: Claimant sold a house before leaving Sri Lanka but has no records of ownership or sale
propositions.quote: They included questions about possible bank records and considering that she sold a house before she left Sri Lanka, records concerning the ownership of the house or the sale of the house...

propositions.text: Claimant never had a driver's license, so no photo ID from that source
propositions.quote: driver's licenses in Sri Lanka are helpful because they are photo identification...The claimant testified that she never had a driver's license, did not drive

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant lacks documents to prove presence in Sri Lanka except one, no house sale records, and no driver's license.

propositions.text: Letter from friend mentions 1992 but no knowledge of claimant in Sri Lanka after that
propositions.quote: The letter from her friend here in Canada mentions 1992; it makes no mention of any knowledge of the claimant being in Sri Lanka after 1992.

propositions.text: Birth certificate lacks photo ID and does not prove presence in Sri Lanka in 2004
propositions.quote: The birth certificate of course is not photo identification, it has no photo identification. It was obtained in XXXXX 2004 but even that does not place her in Sri Lanka in XXXXX 2004 since it is possible to get a copy of your birth certificate in Sri Lanka without being physically present.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the friend’s letter only mentions 1992 and birth certificate lacks photo ID and does not prove presence in 2004.

propositions.text: Received a form letter from attorney with typed personal info, date corrected from 2000 to 2010
propositions.quote: So that leaves the letter from the attorney that I received at the hearing and was printed on XXXXX of either 2000 or 2010, since it has been corrected. It is a form letter and the personal information has been typed on a printed form.

propositions.text: Claimant said attorney was her parent's lawyer, met him by accident in 2009 while grocery shopping
propositions.quote: When the claimant was asked as to how she knew this attorney she testified that it was her parent's attorney. She was asked when she last met this gentleman in Sri Lanka; she testified that she met him by accident in 2009...she testified, in front of the shop.

propositions.text: Claimant never used this lawyer professionally
propositions.quote: But she had never used this lawyer professionally.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the attorney's letter is a form letter with corrected date; claimant met attorney by accident in 2009 and never used him professionally.

propositions.text: If letter had weight, claimant would recall meeting attorney clearly, but she did not
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that if this letter was to be given weight...that the claimant would have been clear in her mind where and when she last met this gentleman and that was clearly not the case in her evidence.

propositions.text: Date correction on letter is suspicious and unnecessary
propositions.quote: Further I am satisfied that the date on the letter would ... there would have been no need to correct that date and particularly not correct it by simply adding a one between the last two zeros of the year 2000.

propositions.text: Attorney would not need to type personal info on form letter
propositions.quote: Further I am satisfied that an attorney, even if it was a form letter today, would not have had to resort to typing the personal information.

propositions.text: Gives letter insufficient weight to offset missing evidence, especially passport
propositions.quote: As a result I give this letter insufficient weight to offset all of the missing evidence, particularly the passport.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's recollection unclear, letter date correction suspicious, and gives letter insufficient weight to offset missing evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant said she gave original passport to agent in Singapore to mail to Canada
propositions.quote: The claimant, when testifying as to the passport, indicated that she gave her original passport to the agent in a house in Singapore with the understanding that he would mail it to an address that she provided him here in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant kept birth certificate for rest of trip from Singapore
propositions.quote: The claimant testified that she kept her birth certificate for the balance of the trip from Singapore.

propositions.text: If agent took passport and ID to avoid conflicting IDs, claimant could have mailed them to herself in Canada
propositions.quote: If the reason that the agent was taking the passport and national identity card from the claimant was that she would not be found with conflicting pieces of identity if searched, then there would be no reason why the claimant could not have simply mailed the national identity card and her passport to herself here in Canada, or if not mailed, sent by courier.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant said she gave passport to agent to mail to Canada, kept birth certificate, but could have mailed passport or ID herself if avoiding conflicting IDs.

propositions.text: Agents use genuine passports to create fraudulent ones but Sri Lankan passport without visa has little value
propositions.quote: Yes, I have heard in other cases agents use genuine passports given by their clients to create fraudulent passports for subsequent clients, but a Sri Lankan passport without a visa would be of little value to the agent who is in the business of moving claimants from Sri Lanka to other countries.

propositions.text: Claimant kept birth certificate thinking she would need it, but passport or ID would be more useful
propositions.quote: The claimant maintains that she kept her birth certificate because she thought she would need it; in reality, either the passport or the national identity card would have much more benefit to the claimant than the birth certificate.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes agents use genuine passports to make fraudulent ones, but Sri Lankan passport without visa is of little value; claimant kept birth certificate but passport or ID more useful.

propositions.text: Agent came with claimant to Canada and likely had passport; both at risk if carrying two IDs
propositions.quote: Further, since the agent came with her to Canada and there is no evidence that he did not bring that passport with him to Canada; he would be equally at risk of having two pieces of identity documents if searched when arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: On balance, claimant did not give passport to agent in Singapore
propositions.quote: On a balance of probability I am satisfied the claimant did not give her passport to an agent in Singapore.

propositions.text: Claimant did not travel to Canada on forged passport as she lacked necessary knowledge
propositions.quote: Further, I am satisfied the claimant did not travel to Canada on a forged passport since she did not know the name of the holder of the passport or any other details that would have been necessary to use a forged passport.

propositions.text: Claimant decided not to divulge her genuine Sri Lankan passport for unknown reasons
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that for some unknown reason the claimant has decided not to divulge her genuine Sri Lankan passport.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds agent likely had passport in Canada; claimant did not give passport to agent or travel on forged passport; claimant chose not to disclose genuine passport.

propositions.text: Claimant indicated unemployed in documents but testified owning grocery store as income source
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked in two areas of her documents for her occupation in Sri Lanka; to the immigration officer and in the Schedule B documents she indicated that she was unemployed...In question 31, in the narrative, paragraph 2, she testified that she owned a grocery store and received an income from it and that was consistent with her oral evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant explained omission of grocery store ownership in documents as forgetfulness
propositions.quote: When asked to explain why she did not indicate that she was a shop owner or some other such indication in the other two areas she testified that it was only a small shop but she agreed it was her only source of income and so when the question was put directly to her that if you owned a small grocery store why not indicate that in both your personal information form and when you were talking to the immigration officer. Her explanation was that she forgot.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant said unemployed in documents but testified owning grocery store; explained omission as forgetfulness.

propositions.text: On balance, claimant likely did not own a XXXXX store in Sri Lanka
propositions.quote: I am satisfied, that on the balance of probabilities, that if the claimant's only source of income in Sri Lanka was as an owner of a small grocery store, that her evidence would be consistent on that point and all parts of her claim and since that is not the case I am satisfied it is more probable than not that she did not own a XXXXX store if she was living in Sri Lanka.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes claimant likely did not own a XXXXX store in Sri Lanka based on inconsistent evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant's travel evidence, passport handling, lack of documents, and employment claims are not credible
propositions.quote: In summary, her evidence as to how she travelled from Sri Lanka to Canada was not credible. Her evidence as to providing the agent with her genuine passport and national identity card so it could be mailed to her later was not credible. Her explanation for having no documents other than the lawyer's letter to support that she was in Sri Lanka at the times after 1992 is implausible. Her answers concerning her employment in Sri Lanka were inconsistent and hence not credible

propositions.text: Claimant failed to establish serious possibility of persecution due to ethnicity or other serious harm
propositions.quote: as a result, on a balance of probability, I find that the claimant was not a credible witness, did not travel to Canada in the way that she described, did not own a XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX and as a result the claimant has failed to establish that there is a serious possibility that she will face persecution due to her ethnicity as a Tamil, born in the north of Sri Lanka or suffer other forms of serious harm.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant not credible on travel, documents, and employment; claimant failed to prove serious risk of persecution or harm.

propositions.text: Refugee Protection Division rejects claim under sections 96 and 97 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
propositions.quote: Hence, the Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim pursuant to both section 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Refugee Protection Division rejects the claim under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
